newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK jobless fall to 5-year low, earnings up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK jobless fall to 5-year low, earnings up.

text.p: British unemployment has tumbled to its lowest level in more than five years but wage inflation ticked higher, a slew of economic figures showed on Wednesday.
A total of 35,600 people were taken off the jobless queues in September, figures from the Office for National Statistics showed -- the largest monthly fall since December 1994.
That took the overall unemployment rate down to 7.4 percent and the total number of jobless, at 2.073 million, to its lowest level since February 1991.
Good news for the unemployed was matched by a boost for those in work. The ONS revised up annual average earnings growth to 4.0 percent in July, from 3.75, and said it held at that level in August.

UK employment minister Eric Forth said the government remained relaxed about wage inflation, despite the pick-up in average earnings. He noted earnings growth has stuck between three and four percent for about three years now.
The opposition Labour Party said 95 percent of new jobs are part-time and the number of full-time employees fell by 47,000 over the summer.

Economists were concerned by the data, not least since September's Public Sector Borrowing Requirement -- the gap between government spending and revenue -- totalled 3.41 billion pounds ($5.41 billion), overshooting market forecasts of a 2.7 billion shortfall.
The PSBR figures were released alongside the jobs data.
"The labour data is worrying, showing signs of strengthening demand for labour feeding through to labour costs," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney.
"It belies the theory that inflation might be dead."
Underlying retail price inflation edged up to 2.9 percent year-on-year in September, sticking stubbornly above the government's 2.5 percent target.

"Although the fall in unemployment is probably exaggerated, the tightness in the labour market is a bit disconcerting because average earnings figures are picking up," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
Britain's public sector deficit will be of at least equal concern to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

He will present his budget, the last before elections which are due by May 1997, on November 26 and members of his ruling Conservative Party are baying for tax cuts to improve their lagging position in opinion polls.
The government has already raised its 1996/97 PSBR forecast to 27 billion pounds from an initial estimate of 22.5 billion. Any further deterioration will eat into the scope for tax cuts.
Nonetheless, analysts said the political realities of an election year mean taxes will be reduced to some degree.

"The Chancellor will still find scope to reduce taxes by a modest amount in the budget," Jeffreys said. He said two to three billion sterling would be taken off income tax with some of that clawed back in areas such as excise duties.
"The PSBR at face value is disappointing but I think it will respond to improving growth and tax revenue flows," he added.

But if Wednesday's data leaves some room for tax cuts, the fall in unemployment and rising earnings surely extinguished any hope of further interest rate cuts -- the other thing Conservative politicians would like to offer disaffected voters.
Jeffreys said the economic situation demanded an interest rate rise this year, not a cut.

But Clarke will be loathe to sanction one even though minutes from recent monetary meetings show Bank of England Governor Eddie George would prefer UK base rates to be raised to 6.00 percent now, from 5.75.

Instead, economists said the government will pin its hopes on the strength of the pound -- at 21-month highs against the mark. That will dampen UK economic activity by pushing up export prices and limit inflation by cutting import prices.

"A hike in base rates is the last thing the government wants pre-election," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica. "We should see an increasingly tolerant policy towards a strong or stronger pound."
